primary_topics: Chapter 9 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' -- CJP's closing report and toast as Centenary Execom chairman, delivered on June 11, 2002, when the Supreme Court's two-year jubilee of more than fifty activities came to a formal close.

He restated the two goals of the celebrations -- to communicate the judiciary's role in nation-building over 100 years and to focus attention and participation on the ongoing judicial reform program -- under the theme 'Katarungan at Bayan Magpakailanman.'

He summarized thirteen completed centenary activities, from the Centenary Lecture Series, the National Speech Festival and the First National Moot Court Competition through publications, regional celebrations, awards, prayers, sportsfests, statues, benchbooks and the mediation pilot, naming the people responsible for each.

He then listed ten ongoing judicial reform projects that would continue after the celebrations ended -- Zero Backlog, new procedural rules, MCLE, computerization, legal-education funding, building renovation and construction, employee housing and the Philja Center -- and closed by accepting responsibility for any imperfections and toasting the Court and its justices.
sub_topics: The frame: celebrations launched June 9, 2000, planned to culminate on the Court's exact 100th birthday of June 11, 2001, extended another year, and formally closing on June 11, 2002.
The honor of chairing the celebrations, and his insistence that their success belonged to those who labored to implement each project rather than to the Execom chairman.

First, the Centenary Lecture Series -- fourteen lectures led by Justice Ameurfina A. Melencio Herrera and coordinated by Dr. Purificacion V. Quisumbing -- ranging from constitutionalism to biotechnology, paperless courts and electronic evidence to Shari'a and Muslim law, and from People Power to the judiciaries of Hungary and Israel.

Second, the National Speech Festival of debates, essays and oratorical contests, organized by the Philippine Association of Law Schools under Dean Hernando B. Perez and then Dean Romulo V. Borja, on the postulate that mastery of forensic and writing skills lets men and women of the law discover truth and render justice.

Third, the First National Moot Court Competition under Undersecretary Merlin M. Magallona -- a simulation of oral arguments before the Supreme Court with unrehearsed interaction between judges and mooters -- which the law schools, the IBP and the law students' association agreed to continue biennially and eventually to fold into the curriculum.

Fourth, the public information and PR programs, including the three-volume Centenary Reader of excerpts from the best Supreme Court decisions, produced at no expense to the Court by Rogelio Pantaleon's 'Legal Write' group with editors led by Justices Abraham F. Sarmiento and Camilo D. Quiason.

Other publications: books on Chief Justices Querube Makalintal and Ramon Avanceña, Justice Cecilia Muñoz-Palma's 'The Mirror of My Soul,' CJP's own 'A Centenary of Justice,' centennial editions of the Philippine Reports and commemorative volumes.

The TV documentary 'Bulwark of Justice' conceptualized under Justice Buena, and the Execom video 'A Celebration of Justice,' which won the Gawad Oscar M. Florendo Award from the Public Relations Organization of the Philippines.

Fifth, celebrations in all judicial regions under Court Administrator Alfredo L. Benipayo, acting Court Administrator Zenaida N. Elepaño and Court Administrator Presbitero J. Velasco Jr. with the executive judges and the Philippine Judges Association, with parades, sports and cultural programs zeroing in on reform as it applied to the trial courts.

Sixth, centennial awards to retired magistrates at a Manila Hotel luncheon, with a Book and Photo Exhibit organized by the Association of Retired Supreme Court Justices under Justice Abraham F. Sarmiento.

Seventh, ecumenical services and Masses, and the 'Centennial Prayer for the Courts' composed by the Execom after consultation with all major religious denominations and now recited in all courts nationwide.

Eighth and ninth, the Judiciary Sportsfest of tennis and golf under Execom Vice Chairman Justice Leonardo A. Quisumbing, the employees' Centennial Sportsfest, and a cultural program and luncheon for Supreme Court employees with awards to outstanding former employees.

Tenth, the once-in-a-hundred-years Centennial Awards for Judicial Excellence after a nationwide search led by Senior Justice Josue N. Bellosillo and Justice Jose Y. Feria, with top RTC awardee Judge Mario L. Guarina III promoted to the appellate court.

Eleventh, the commissioned statues of Chief Justices Cayetano Arellano and Jose Abad Santos for the front courtyard and murals of the Court's history for the main lobby, supervised with the Centenary Reader by the Philippine Judiciary Foundation under Justice Carolina Griño-Aquino.

Twelfth, the Benchbook for Judges and Benchbook on Penalties, funded by the Australian government and the Asia Foundation and now called the bibles of judges, with Philja training courses on their use.

Thirteenth, mediation: the Settlement Week pilot in Manila, Cebu and Davao from March 26 to April 6, 2001, in which 1,469 of 1,816 referred cases -- 81 percent -- were settled, leading to the establishment of the Philippine Mediation Center on April 6, 2001.

Ongoing reform projects: the Zero Backlog program to decide all cases within the constitutional twenty-four months, followed by the Court of Appeals under Presiding Justice Ma. Alicia Austria-Martinez and by Court Administrator Velasco for the trial courts.

The Committee on Rules under Justice Reynato S. Puno updating the Rules on Criminal Procedure and issuing new rules on electronic evidence, corporate rehabilitation, juveniles in conflict with the law, family disputes and intellectual property.

The MCLE Board under Justice Carolina Griño-Aquino, aimed at elevating the professional and ethical standards of lawyers; the purchase and distribution of 1,500 computers with Lex Libris monitored by Justice Consuelo Y. Santiago; and the Foundation for the Enhancement of Legal Education under Atty. Ricardo J. Romulo raising funds for professorial chairs and scholarships.

The physical program: renovation of the Session Hall, conference rooms, lobby and courtyard under Justice Vicente V. Mendoza; the completed Centennial Building inaugurated that morning; the Committee on Halls of Justice under Justice Santiago M. Kapunan supervising the model Manila Hall of Justice at the old Jai Alai Fronton and a parking building; and Baguio cottages replacing those destroyed by the earthquake ten years earlier.

The employees' mass housing program taken over by Justice Antonio T. Carpio on Justice Bernardo P. Pardo's retirement, to be built in Cavite with GSIS and Pag-ibig assistance along the planned LRT extension; and the P500-million Philja Center in Tagaytay under Chief Justice Davide and Chancellor Melencio Herrera.

The close: a fuller account promised in the Centenary Yearbook prepared by Atty. Ismael G. Khan Jr.'s Public Information Office, thanks to Chief Justice Davide and his colleagues, personal acceptance of responsibility for imperfections, credit to the Court and the Execom, thanks to the Lord Jesus Christ, and a toast to the Supreme Court and its justices.

stances.claim: The centennial celebrations succeeded not because of the Execom chairman but because of the hundreds of men and women inside and outside the court system who steadfastly and persistently labored to carry out every project envisioned.
stances.rhetorical_move: credit-deflection: a chairman's report built almost entirely out of other people's names

stances.claim: The celebrations were justified by their two purposes -- communicating the judiciary's role in nation-building and focusing participation on the ongoing judicial reform program -- rather than by commemoration for its own sake, which is why the report ends with ten reform projects that will continue after the jubilee closes.
stances.rhetorical_move: purpose-over-pageantry framing, enacted structurally by pivoting from completed celebrations to unfinished reform

stances.claim: Mediation works as a tool for decongesting court dockets, as the Settlement Week pilot showed by settling 1,469 of 1,816 referred cases -- 81 percent -- which justified institutionalizing it in the Philippine Mediation Center.
stances.rhetorical_move: pilot-to-institution argument carried by a single settlement statistic

stances.claim: Although all the centennial projects were acclaimed as successful, some may not have been perfect, and he personally accepts responsibility for all the imperfections while giving the credit for success to the Court and the Executive Committee.
stances.rhetorical_move: asymmetric accounting of blame and credit -- 'the buck stops at the desk of the Execom chairman'

notable_anecdotes: He announced proudly that the Execom's video presentation 'A Celebration of Justice' had been given the prestigious Gawad Oscar M. Florendo Award by the Public Relations Organization of the Philippines.

He acknowledged publicly that the three-volume Centenary Reader was produced at no expense to the Court by Rogelio Pantaleon's 'Legal Write' group, with editors led by Justices Abraham F. Sarmiento and Camilo D. Quiason.

As a measure of the esteem attached to the Centennial Awards for Judicial Excellence, he noted that Judge Mario L. Guarina III, the top awardee among regional trial court judges, had recently been promoted to the appellate court.
He reported the Settlement Week results with evident satisfaction: 1,469 of the 1,816 cases referred for mediation, or 81 percent, were successfully settled in the Manila, Cebu and Davao pilot.
He mentioned that two additional cottages were being built in the Court's Baguio compound to replace the ones destroyed by the earthquake ten years earlier, with the staff house nearly finished.

He noted that the Centennial Prayer for the Courts, composed by the Execom after consultation with all the major religious denominations and recited at the beginning of that very program, is now used in all courts across the country.

He closed by accepting personal responsibility for any imperfections -- 'the buck stops at the desk of the Execom chairman' -- thanking the Lord Jesus Christ, and raising a toast to the Supreme Court as 'the bulwark of justice, the conscience of society, the guardian of the Constitution and the seat of freedom in our land.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 9 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' reproduced Justice Panganiban's closing report and toast as chairman of the Centenary Executive Committee, delivered on June 11, 2002, as the Supreme Court's two-year jubilee -- launched June 9, 2000, meant to culminate on the Court's exact 100th birthday of June 11, 2001, and then extended a year -- came to a formal close. He restated the celebrations' two goals, to communicate the judiciary's role in nation-building over a century and to focus participation on the ongoing reform program, under the theme 'Katarungan at Bayan Magpakailanman,' and insisted that their success belonged not to the Execom chairman but to the hundreds who implemented each project. He then summarized thirteen activities: the fourteen-lecture Centenary Lecture Series led by Justice Ameurfina A. Melencio Herrera, spanning constitutionalism, biotechnology, paperless courts, Shari'a law, People Power and foreign judiciaries; the National Speech Festival run by the law deans; the First National Moot Court Competition under Undersecretary Merlin M. Magallona, which the law schools, IBP and student association agreed to continue biennially; public-information work including the three-volume Centenary Reader produced at no cost to the Court, books on past Chief Justices, and the award-winning video 'A Celebration of Justice'; regional celebrations under the court administrators; awards and an exhibit for retired magistrates; ecumenical services and the Centennial Prayer for the Courts now recited nationwide; judiciary and employee sportsfests; a cultural program for Supreme Court employees; the Centennial Awards for Judicial Excellence, whose top trial-court awardee had just been promoted; commissioned statues of Chief Justices Arellano and Abad Santos and murals of the Court's history; the Australian- and Asia Foundation-funded Benchbooks now called the bibles of judges; and the Settlement Week mediation pilot, which settled 1,469 of 1,816 referred cases and led to the Philippine Mediation Center. He then listed ten continuing reform projects -- Zero Backlog, new procedural rules under Justice Puno, the MCLE Board, 1,500 computers with Lex Libris, a legal-education foundation, building renovations, the new Centennial Building and Halls of Justice, Baguio cottages, employee mass housing, and the P500-million Philja Center in Tagaytay -- before accepting personal responsibility for any imperfections, crediting the Court and Execom for the successes, thanking the Lord Jesus Christ, and toasting the Court as the bulwark of justice and its justices as pillars of integrity, independence, intelligence and industry.
